    "1/3 cup minced yellow onions",

  "recipeInstructions": [
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 1,
      "name": "Cook the onions",
      "text": "Cook the onions slowly in butter in a small saucepan for 5 minutes or so, until tender and translucent but not browned. Stir in the shallots or onions, and garlic, and cook slowly for 1 minute more. Set aside.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 2,
      "name": "Prepare the scallops",
      "text": "Dry the scallops and cut into slices 1/4 inch thick. Just before cooking, sprinkle with salt and pepper, roll in flour, and shake off excess flour.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 3,
      "name": "Saut\u00e9 the scallops",
      "text": "Saut\u00e9 the scallops quickly in very hot butter and oil for 2 minutes to brown them lightly.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 4,
      "name": "Simmer with wine and herbs",
      "text": "Pour the wine, or the vermouth and water, into the skillet with the scallops. Add the herbs and the cooked onion mixture. Cover the skillet and simmer for 5 minutes. Then uncover, and if necessary boil down the sauce rapidly for a minute until it is lightly thickened. Correct seasoning, and discard bay leaf.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 5,
      "name": "Fill the shells",
      "text": "Spoon the scallops and sauce into the shells. Sprinkle with cheese and dot with butter. Set aside or refrigerate until ready to gratin\u00e9.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 6,
      "name": "Broil and serve",
      "text": "Just before serving, run under a moderately hot broiler for 3 to 4 minutes to heat through, and to brown the cheese lightly.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    }
  ],
  "notes": "Julia's version of Coquilles Saint Jacques can be prepared in advance and gratin\u00e9ed just before serving. The proportions given are sufficient for a first course. Double them for a main course. Serve a chilled ros\u00e9, or a dry white such as C\u00f4tes de Provence. This recipe is excerpted from Mastering the Art of French Cooking by Julia Child.     "story": "Coquilles Saint Jacques emerged in medieval France as a pilgrimage dish, its name invoking Saint James (Jacques) and the scallop shell that became his symbol. The dish evolved from humble coastal fare into a refined preparation during the 18th and 19th centuries, when French chefs began layering scallops with wine-based sauces and gratin\u00e9ing them under a golden crust of breadcrumbs and butter. The technique became canonical in classical French cuisine, codified in the grand kitchens of Paris and the Loire Valley.\n\nThe dish belongs quintessentially to the Atlantic coast of France \u2014 Brittany and Normandy in particular \u2014 where scallops (called coquilles) are harvested in abundance and white wine production supports the wine-and-cream sauces that define the region's seafood cookery. The dish is often presented in the scallop shell itself, a theatrical touch that connects the plate to its maritime heritage.
